beats.text: Some commands you use every day. Others, only {now}now and then. For those, you don't need to {remember}remember a single hotkey.
Let's {qm}open a QuickMenu, {build}build your own, and {search}find anything with the launcher.
Sometimes, one key per command isn't enough. That's what {qm}QuickMenus are for.
Press a hotkey, say {mouse5}Mouse 5, and a menu {blooms}blooms right where your pointer is. Translucent, with {icons}icons, {titles}titles, {separators}separators and {submenus}submenus.

{left}Left click runs a command and closes the menu. {right}Right click runs it and keeps the menu open, perfect for {nudging}nudging the volume. {middle}Middle click jumps straight to editing that item. And the whole menu works from the {keyboard}keyboard, too.

Menus are built in the {editor}editor. {drag}Drag commands from the palette onto the menu: {above}above, {below}below, or {inside}inside an item. {rename}Rename, change icons, {nest}nest submenus, {undo}undo and redo, and choose a {size}size, from compact to huge.
Need something new? A {quick}quick command turns a {program}program, a {folder}folder or a {web}web address into a menu item, in one step.
For everything else, there's the {launcher}launcher: a search box with its own {hotkey}hotkey.
Type a few letters, even loose ones. {c}C, M, F, Y finds {comfy}ComfyUI. It searches your {commands}commands and every program in the {start}Start menu, {store}Store apps included.
Type a {sum}sum, and it's a calculator: {enter}Enter copies the result. And when {nothing}nothing matches, it offers to {web}search the web.
It learns what you use {most}most, and puts it first, before you even {type}type.
It finds {files}files and folders too, from the Windows index. Type a {question}question mark first to search only files, and {ctrl}Control Enter opens the folder they're in.
It even searches your {clipboard}clipboard history: pick something you copied, and Enter {pastes}pastes it. Each of these can be {switch}switched on or off, in Settings, Launcher.
And your {menus}QuickMenus go with you: on your {phone}phone, the web app and the Android app show them, ready to tap.

One last tip: a command {nokey}doesn't need a hotkey at all. Give it a clear name, and {launcher}run it from the launcher with a few letters. Like {steam}Steam, {headphones}Switch to headphones, or {lights}Living room lights off. Even {hidden}hidden commands can show up there, if you turn that on.
